name: Tokutei JAS jidori standard (jidori definition)
text: Under the MAFF-explained Specific JAS standard, a bird may be sold as jidori only if at least 50% of its blood is from a designated native breed (an 'zairaishu' established or introduced and settled in Japan by the Meiji era) with provable birth records, is raised 75 days or longer, is kept on the floor (free-range style) from 28 days of age, and is kept at no more than 10 birds per square metre from 28 days.
flavor: Used on menus and invoices as a legal-grade claim; implies firmer, slower-grown meat than broiler (wakadori).
use: Check the term when buying: 'jidori' is a standard-bound label, whereas 'meigara-dori' (branded chicken) is not the same category.
craft: Sources differ on the minimum rearing period: MAFF's explanation gives 75 days, while the Yamagata prefectural manual gives 80 days or more from hatching for its own brand. Individual brands (Hinai, Satsuma) set longer periods and lower densities than the JAS floor, so ask the supplier for the brand's own rule rather than assuming the minimum.

name: Hinai Jidori (Akita)
text: Akita's flagship jidori, developed by the prefectural livestock station by crossing the Hinai-dori (a national natural monument) with Rhode Island Red. It was completed in 1977 (Showa 52) and reached the market as food meat from 1978. One of the 'three great jidori' with Nagoya Cochin and Satsuma jidori.
flavor: Firm, deeply flavoured meat; the brand is associated with a strong savoury broth (kiritanpo-nabe, oyako-don).
use: Grilled, in nabe and soup, and as oyako-don; whole birds and parts are sold by sex and age.
craft: Brand rules reported by a tourism article: hens raised 150 days or more and males 100 days or more, at 5 birds per square metre or less, roughly double the JAS minimum rearing time. Because the long rearing is the quality basis, confirm sex and age on delivery; one retailer describes the cross as Hinai-dori male with Rhode Island Red female, which is a single seller's statement.
src: Hinai Jidori Factory: Hinai jidori and Hinai-dori

name: Hinai-dori (Hinai fowl, natural monument)
text: The native Akita fowl designated a national natural monument in 1942 (Showa 17). Because it has weak fertility and disease resistance it did not suit commercial production, so the Akita livestock research station worked on an edible improvement by crossing it with Rhode Island Red, which produced the Hinai Jidori.
flavor: Not sold as a meat bird; its value is as the genetic basis of the jidori.
use: Reference breed: explains why Hinai Jidori is a cross and why pure Hinai-dori is not on the market.
craft: When a menu or retailer says 'Hinai-dori' check whether they mean the protected pure fowl or the Hinai Jidori cross; only the latter is a commercial food product.
src: Hinai Jidori Factory: Hinai jidori and Hinai-dori

name: Nagoya Cochin
text: A breed developed by the Kaibe brothers, former Owari samurai, by crossing native fowl with Buff Cochin. On 10 March 1905 (Meiji 38) the Japan Poultry Association certified it as the first domestic practical breed. Sources disagree on when the work began, one saying about 1882 and another early Meiji.
flavor: Rich, savoury meat; also a dual-purpose bird that lays eggs.
use: Counted among the three great jidori; used for grilling, nabe, oyako-don and its eggs.
craft: Aichi Prefecture's own pages describe its history and traits. Verify whether a product is purebred Nagoya Cochin or a jidori with Cochin sire; one trade article distinguishes the strict purebred (both parents Nagoya Cochin) from crosses with a Cochin father, but its reliability should be checked per supplier.
src: Aichi Pref.: Nagoya Cochin history and traits

name: Nagoya Cochin eggs
text: Eggs of the Nagoya Cochin are known for a sakura-pink shell, sometimes with white speckles. Compared with white-shell eggs, the yolk is darker and more viscous, and an Aichi Prefecture taste-sensor study reported higher umami and richness. The hens lay fewer eggs than common layers, so the eggs are a premium item.
flavor: Deeper yolk colour, thick yolk, rich umami; the white is said to whip well.
use: Tamago kake gohan, oyako-don (one restaurant uses four eggs per bowl), confectionery.
craft: Seller claims such as 'twice the umami of ordinary eggs' have uneven support; rely on the Aichi sensor result and judge by yolk firmness and colour on the plate. Low laying rate means supply and price are less stable than for commodity eggs.
src: Nagoya Cochin egg vs other eggs (Toyohashi Shiryo)

name: Satsuma Jidori (Kagoshima)
text: Kagoshima's jidori, ranked among the three great jidori. It carries the blood of the Satsuma-dori, a native fowl designated a national natural monument. Reported rearing time is 120 to 150 days.
flavor: Firm, well-flavoured meat in the same class as Hinai and Nagoya Cochin.
use: Grilled, sashimi-style tataki and nabe in Kagoshima; sold as whole birds and parts.
craft: Search sources confirmed only the natural-monument bloodline and the 120-150 day figure, not the exact cross; ask the producer for the breed formula and day count. Do not assume Satsuma-dori the pure breed is the food product.

name: Okukuji Shamo (Ibaraki)
text: A shamo (gamecock) brand of Ibaraki. The shamo was imported from Siam in the Edo period as a fighting bird, and its aggressiveness was a problem; the Ibaraki poultry experiment station improved it to reduce fighting spirit and raise fertility, giving the Okukuji Shamo. The meat is described as firm and low in fat.
flavor: Tight, chewy, lean meat with little fat.
use: Nabe and grilled dishes in the Okukuji area (Daigo town).
craft: Lean, firm meat tolerates longer cooking in nabe but overcooks quickly on the grill; judge doneness by resilience rather than time. Detail on exact crossing and rearing days was not in the sources seen.

name: Tosa-Jiro (Kochi)
text: A first-generation cross between the Tosa jidori (a natural monument native fowl of Kochi) male and Rhode Island Red female, developed at the Kochi livestock research station. It is a dual-purpose meat-and-egg bird. The name comes from 'ji' of jidori and 'ro' of Rhode Island Red.
flavor: Low fat, with umami that builds with chewing.
use: Sold as meat and as eggs (for example the Tosayama brand egg 'Kimi ga ii').
craft: Because it is a first cross, quality depends on keeping the parent lines pure; the Japan Chicken Association page is the best check for brand rules. Eggs and meat from the same flock are marketed separately.

name: Amakusa Daio (Kumamoto)
text: A very large meat fowl developed in the Amakusa area from Langshan birds imported from China in the mid-Meiji period. It was once popular for Hakata mizutaki, died out in the early Showa period and was restored by Kumamoto Prefecture in the 2000s. The current meat bird crosses a restored male with a Kyushu Road hen. Males are reported to reach about 90 cm in height.
flavor: Large-framed bird; meat described as suited to long-simmered dishes such as mizutaki.
use: Mizutaki and grill, sold as a Kumamoto brand.
craft: The Kumamoto prefectural page explains the restoration and the production cross; since this is a restored breed with a hybrid commercial bird, confirm the sire/dam formula with the producer.

name: Yamagata Jidori
text: Yamagata's own jidori brand, managed by the Yamagata Jidori Promotion Council with the prefectural agricultural research center's livestock station, with a rearing manual under a registered trademark. The manual sets a minimum rearing period of 80 days from hatching.
flavor: Not described in the source seen.
use: Brand poultry supplied under a documented rearing manual.
craft: The 80-day rule is the brand's own and is longer than the 75 days that MAFF's explanation gives for the JAS minimum, which shows why brand rules, not the JAS floor, are the thing to audit.

name: Kagoshima Kurobuta (Berkshire)
text: Kagoshima's black pig. One account traces it to pigs brought from the Ryukyus by Shimazu Iehisa about 400 years ago, with Berkshire introduced from England in the early Meiji era to drive breed improvement. Since the 1999 revision of the retail meat quality standard, only purebred Berkshire may be labelled 'kurobuta', though one source phrases the rule differently.
flavor: Firm, sweet fat and dense lean, as generally described by the brand association.
use: Shabu-shabu, tonkatsu, kakuni, grilling; the Kagoshima Kurobuta association promotes the term.
craft: Check that the label says purebred Berkshire; white three-way crosses cannot legally be sold as kurobuta. Sources seen do not give feed or finishing days, so ask each farm.
src: Kurobuta: only purebred Berkshire (Tokyo Pork Plus)

name: Rokuhaku-buta (six-white pig)
text: Another name for the Berkshire pig: it has white markings at six points, including the nose and the feet. The breed originates in Berkshire in south-east England and was substantially improved in the late 18th to early 19th century by crossing with small black pigs imported from Asia.
flavor: Spoken term on menus and in pork trade, 'rokuhaku' for Berkshire.
use: Used on menus and by farms to signal Berkshire/kurobuta.
craft: The six white points help visually identify purebred stock; on carcass, rely on paperwork instead.

name: Sangen-buta (three-way cross pork)
text: The standard supermarket pork in Japan: a three-breed cross of Landrace, Large White (Yorkshire) and Duroc. These are the white-skinned breeds, in contrast to purebred black Berkshire.
flavor: Mild, leaner baseline pork.
use: Labels such as 'sangen-buta' tell you the cross, not a regional brand.
craft: Brands built on sangen-buta differ by feed, cross order and finishing, so ask which breed is on the sire side.

name: Kokusan Gibier Ninsho (domestic game certification)
text: A MAFF scheme created in May 2018 that certifies facilities processing wild-caught deer and boar. Only game caught in Japan qualifies; the facility must be run by a business holding a meat processing licence under Food Sanitation Act Article 55, follow the MHLW wild-game hygiene guideline, and use a nationally unified cut chart for part names.
flavor: Regulatory term, not a flavour.
use: Chefs can use the certification to source traceable venison and boar.
craft: Certification covers deer and boar only; bear, pheasant and others fall outside it. Hygiene control and cut naming are the audited points.
src: MAFF press release on the certification

name: Chinuki and aging of game (gibier)
text: For wild game, the chain from dismantling through bleeding, freezing and thawing strongly affects off-odours. Bleeding methods described by processors include massaging the arteries after exsanguination. Some processors age meat per individual animal, and one gives dry aging at about one week to ten days.
flavor: Clean bleeding reduces blood off-flavours; aging is said to raise umami and tenderness.
use: Ask the processor for bleeding time and aging method before ordering.
craft: These are individual company practices, not an official standard. Judge by the colour of the lean, absence of blood smell and drip when cut.

name: Kumamoto horse meat (baniku)
text: Kumamoto is Japan's top horse meat producer: 2,316 tonnes in the FY2015 MAFF survey. Legend says Kato Kiyomasa's army ate war horses during the Korean campaign and found them delicious, though this is treated as a later story. Many horses raised in Kumamoto were born in Canada or Hokkaido. Reported national share varies by source, about 40 to 45 percent.
flavor: Lean red meat, eaten raw as basashi.
use: Basashi and other cuts; sold nationwide.
craft: 'Kumamoto' on a label can mean fattened there rather than born there, and the share statistics differ by year, so cite the year and survey.

name: Aizu horse meat (Fukushima)
text: Horse meat in Aizu is said to have been valued from the Edo period, with the Boshin War giving a push when it was fed to wounded soldiers. Lean red meat is the norm and it is eaten with karashi miso (mustard miso).
flavor: Lean meat served with pungent karashi miso.
use: Basashi with karashi miso, and local dishes.
craft: The karashi miso pairing cuts through the lean meat; Aizu is one of the three major horse meat regions with Kumamoto and Nagano.

name: Nagano horse meat
text: In Nagano, horse meat is tied to using working farm horses fully and to the Shio no Michi (salt road) pack-horse trade. Production is small, about 4 percent of the national total and fifth in rank in one source, though one blog claims consumption is second in Japan, which could not be confirmed by statistics.
flavor: Lean red meat, eaten raw and cooked.
use: Basashi and local cooking in Nagano.
craft: Consumption ranking claims are not backed by statistics in the sources seen; do not quote them as fact.

name: Koshiki hogei at Taiji (traditional whaling, history)
text: Taiji in Wakayama began organised whaling in 1606 (Keicho 11) when Wada Chubei Yorimoto and others used the tsukitori (thrust) method; the net method (amitori) was introduced in 1675 and expanded the industry. The Japan Heritage story also names Miwasaki and Kozagawa as whaling sites.
flavor: Historical term.
use: Context for regional whale cuisine in Wakayama.
craft: Whaling-group roles at Taiji were reportedly hereditary, which shaped the town's tradition. History only: this entry does not cover current catch rules.
src: Mizu no Bunka: whaling and craft diffusion

name: Shimonoseki as whale distribution hub
text: In the Edo period Shimonoseki was a collection and distribution centre for whale meat. Whale meat and oil from Choshu whaling went through Shimonoseki wholesalers to Kansai, Hokuriku and Kyushu, and northern Kyushu was a large consuming area.
flavor: Historical term.
use: Explains the western Japan whale food culture, including the Shimonoseki-Kitakyushu area.
craft: Edible parts went through the Kanmon Strait to the Seto Inland Sea coast and Osaka.

name: Whale parts in Japanese cuisine: une and sarashi-kujira
ja: 畝（うね）とさらしくじら
text: Japanese whale cookery used the whole animal. The ventral groove (une), skin and meat, was made into bacon, and the skin of the tail fluke became sarashi-kujira (blanched whale skin). After the war, whale meat was a cheap source of protein and used in school lunches, according to the Japan Whaling Association.
flavor: Historical cuisine terms.
use: Historical reference for menus that cite whale.
craft: Part names differ by source; treat blog descriptions of tail cuts as unverified.

name: Aigamo duck and aigamo rice-duck farming
text: Aigamo broadly means domesticated mallard or a duck-mallard hybrid; commonly it is the first cross of mallard and domestic duck. Much meat sold as aigamo is in practice domestic duck. Ducks arrived around the Heian period; in 1991 Furuno Takao, an organic farmer in Fukuoka, established combined duck-and-rice farming (aigamo suitoh) and a national association was founded the same year.
flavor: Duck-style red meat with fat.
use: Kamo nanban, nabe, roast breast.
craft: The names mallard, duck and aigamo are commercial, not strict biological categories, so ask the supplier for breed and rearing; an article states true hybrid ducks are small and rarely raised for meat.

name: Yukijirushi Hokkaido Butter
text: Launched in 1925 (Taisho 14), when 629 dairy farmers invested in the Hokkaido Seiraku Hanbai Kumiai (predecessor of Megmilk Snow Brand); its first product was butter, under the Yukijirushi trademark. It is a long-seller with a brand site.
flavor: Standard Hokkaido-style salted butter.
use: Table, baking and cooking butter; an unsalted version exists.
craft: Source detail on churning method is not given in the pages seen; for bakery use compare the unsalted product's spec sheet.

name: Atsubetsu Bokujo Butter (Shin-Sapporo Milk)
ja: 北海道厚別牧場バター
text: A butter by Shin-Sapporo Milk, in production since 1958 and made by the traditional combined-churn method.
flavor: Traditional-style butter.
use: Table and cooking.
craft: The combined churn (churning and working in one machine) is the process claim to ask the maker about.

name: Yotsuba Hokkaido butter and milk
text: Yotsuba treats butter as its origin product, made since the founding of its predecessor, Hokkaido Kyodo Nyugyo. The company has brand sites for Hokkaido butter and milk.
flavor: Not described in the pages seen.
use: Retail butter and milk.
craft: Specification details are not in the snippets seen; consult the maker's brand pages.

name: Hokkaido natural cheese (history)
ja: 北海道のナチュラルチーズ
text: Hokkaido's cheese story names Edwin Dun as the 'father of Hokkaido dairy farming'. The Hokkaido dairy federation (Rakuren) built a plant at Asabu, Yufutsu district, in 1933 (Showa 8) and began full-scale cheese production.
flavor: Not described in the pages seen.
use: Historical background for Hokkaido's cheese workshops.
craft: Nagano and Tochigi cheese makers were not covered by the search results, so no claims are made here.
